candidates.attacker_control: The filePath argument is the value a consuming application gates on (typically a user-supplied filename/relative path combined with baseDirPath). The attacker chooses the path, including '..' segments and/or a target whose directory name extends the base directory string.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Canonical paths are used, so classic symlink and plain '..' escapes that land in a non-prefix-sharing directory are still detected (method returns true/safe); the flaw is limited to the prefix-adjacent case, but that case is exactly what a raw startsWith cannot distinguish. The reverse error direction (reporting outside as inside) is fail-safe. @NonNull annotations only guard nulls. No in-repo caller exists, so exploitability depends on consumer usage, which cannot be verified from this snapshot. The method's own javadoc asserts an inside/outside guarantee that line 25 does not implement.
candidates.impact: Bypass of a directory-confinement/sanitizer helper: files outside the intended directory ('..' sibling with a name sharing the base prefix) can be read or overwritten, e.g. exposing configuration/credential files or corrupting files outside the upload/working directory. Since the method is the library's advertised path-traversal remediation, downstream applications relying on it silently lose that protection.
candidates.prerequisites: A consumer of the library uses isFileOutsideDir(...) as its confinement check before opening/reading/writing files, and the attacker can influence the filePath (directly or via traversal segments) while a prefix-sharing sibling directory is reachable/nameable. No such caller exists in this snapshot, so the flaw is only reachable through downstream consumers of this public utility method.
candidates.root_cause: isFileOutsideDir returns !file.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(baseDir.getCanonicalPath()). String.startsWith performs a character-prefix test with no requirement that the following character be a path separator (or end of string). Any sibling path whose absolute name begins with the base directory string is therefore classified as inside the base directory. Canonicalization correctly resolves '.'/'..' and symlinks, but it cannot compensate for the missing separator boundary; there is also no case-normalization for case-insensitive filesystems.
candidates.title: Directory containment bypass in FileSecurityUtils.isFileOutsideDir due to raw prefix comparison of canonical paths
candidates.trace: Example: baseDirPath = '/srv/uploads'; attacker-controlled filePath = '/srv/uploads/../uploads_backup/secret.conf' (or the caller concatenates baseDir + '../uploads_backup/secret.conf'). file.getCanonicalPath() = '/srv/uploads_backup/secret.conf'; baseDir.getCanonicalPath() = '/srv/uploads'; '/srv/uploads_backup/secret.conf'.startsWith('/srv/uploads') == true, so the method returns false = 'file is inside the base dir' (see javadoc at lines 14-19). The caller proceeds to operate on a file that actually resides outside the intended base directory.
candidates.unverified: No runtime test was executed and there are no callers/tests in this snapshot, so the exact downstream sink (read/write/delete) and the attacker's ability to reach a prefix-sharing sibling path are inferred from the method contract, not observed. Windows case-insensitive behavior and separator handling were reasoned from File/startsWith semantics, not executed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Path Traversal / improper path-containment check (prefix match without separator boundary)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the full 7-file snapshot (all source files read line-by-line: Encoder.java 410 lines, FileSecurityUtils.java, SecureObjectInputStream.java, WssAllowListForLog.json, pom.xml, README.md, .gitignore). P1 relation index reports 7/7 source files indexed, 41 symbols, 70 edges, zero missing files; the index shows no internal callers of isFileOutsideDir and no test sources, and relation facts are navigation-only. Sink-level callers of the public sanitizers are outside this repository, which is stated as a limitation.
limitations: No build, test, or execution was performed; findings are source-level only.

The repository contains no application code or tests that call the public utility methods, so downstream usage (which method guards which file operation, and whether the whitelist/encoders are used as documented) is unverified.
The P1 relation index is syntactic navigation only, with unresolved call sites (e.g., String.startsWith, FilenameUtils.normalize) and no data-flow, reachability, or exploitability proof.
Path-comparison behavior on case-insensitive filesystems (Windows) and OS separator specifics were reasoned from Java semantics, not executed.
No external advisories, patches, or CVE data were consulted, per instructions.

rejected_leads.lead: SecureObjectInputStream.isSubpackage (lines 60-68) matches package prefixes with startsWith and derives the package via FilenameUtils.removeExtension; resolveProxyClass is not overridden.
rejected_leads.reason: The prefix match could allow a class in package 'com.examplefoo' when 'com.example' is whitelisted, but exploitation needs a gadget class already on the classpath in a prefix-matching package, and the javadoc explicitly documents that subpackages are allowed. Proxy descriptors bypass resolveClass, but the InvocationHandler class still traverses resolveClass. Config-dependent, no in-repo proof of a gadget class or vulnerable caller.

rejected_leads.lead: Encoder.replaceForbiddenCharsWithSafeChar (lines 68-74) concatenates allow-list entries into a regex character class without escaping, and uses safeCharReplacement as a regex replacement ($ and \ are special).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires the attacker to control the JSON allow-list file content; the path is chosen by the caller and normally trusted configuration. No attacker-controlled configuration path demonstrated in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Default allow list WssAllowListForLog.json permits \u000A/\u000D and other line separators, and Encoder.forLogContent (lines 147-156) only replaces literal \n/\r/\t, so log-line forging may survive 'log sanitization'.
rejected_leads.reason: Intent is ambiguous (whitespace may be deliberately allowed), no sink or downstream log consumer is present in the snapshot, so impact cannot be established from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: Encoder.forCrlf (lines 188-196) misses form feed, vertical tab, NEL, U+2028/U+2029 and double-encoded/percent-obfuscated CRLF variants.
rejected_leads.reason: Sanitizer-coverage gap depends on the downstream consumer's handling of those characters; no proven header/log sink in this repository.

rejected_leads.lead: Encoder.forOsCommand / encodeCharacterForOsCommand (lines 112-121, 381-393) rely on backslash (Unix) / caret (Windows) escaping that is context-sensitive (fails inside quotes; cmd.exe % and ! expansion; backslash-newline continuation).
rejected_leads.reason: Shell-escaping correctness depends entirely on how callers embed the value (quoting context), which is not present in the snapshot; no concrete injection trace can be closed from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: AllowListProperties (Encoder.java lines 76-89) has only private fields/constructor and getters, with no setters, so Jackson field population may fail and cause a RuntimeException.
rejected_leads.reason: This is at most an availability/robustness concern (fail-closed) and depends on Jackson visibility configuration I cannot execute or verify here; not a security-boundary bypass.

summary: The snapshot is the small CureKit Java sanitization library (7 files, all read: pom.xml, README, .gitignore, Encoder.java, FileSecurityUtils.java, SecureObjectInputStream.java, WssAllowListForLog.json). The strongest source-evidenced issue is the path-containment check in FileSecurityUtils.isFileOutsideDir (line 25): it decides "inside/outside" with a raw String.startsWith on canonical paths, so a sibling path that shares the base directory's textual prefix (e.g. base /srv/uploads, file /srv/uploads_backup/secret) is reported as inside the base dir, letting a consumer that relies on this gate read/write outside the intended directory. Other sanitizer/whitelist weaknesses were examined but depend on configuration or caller context and are recorded as rejected leads.
